item.page_text:
Gravel ‘n Granite is returning to Tenterfield, NSW, from March 5-7, 2027. Touring the granite-strewn hills around town, the courses are built on adventure. While there are some open, champagne gravel roads, you should also expect rugged climbs, technical descents, and most of all, amazing, ever-changing scenery.
We packed up the Flowmobile to ride the last edition of Gravel ‘n Granite and to see what Tenterfield was all about. Waiting there for us was a mega-fun festival vibe, a challenging ride and an awesome preview of the terrain the upcoming Angry Bull Trails project will traverse.
We caught up with Caitlin Reid from the Saddlers MTB Club to find out what’s planned in 2027.
In 2027, Gravel ‘n Granite is offering four distance options run across the weekend. The three longer courses will run on Saturday morning (March 6), and the shorter family ride will set off on Sunday morning (March 7).
According to Reid, the routes remain unchanged from the last edition, in all of their rugged, rough-and-tumble goodness. However, this year, the Range Rumble, Wellington Rocks and Currys Gap rides will have a rolling start behind a vehicle escort from the showground.
Reid also tells Flow that the event village will be set in a new area of the showground called the Woolshed for a more intimate vibe, with food trucks, coffee, beer and wine, fire pits, and a DJ playing all day.
The Range Rumble is the headliner of Gravel ‘n Granite with a 91km loop. According to the Strava route, there is over 2,000m of climbing, but my Wahoo logged 1,884m of ascent on the ride. Even so, that is a lotta vert!
The route is about 60% off-road, with basically the entire back half a mix of open gravel roads, double track, rutted 4WD trails, fire roads, and everything in between, through Basket Swamp and Boonoo Boonoo National Parks.
It’s well and truly a mountain biker’s gravel event and will challenge both your fitness and technical ability. But don’t forget to keep your head up and look around. Your surroundings are constantly changing, and it’s one of the most scenic gravel rides I’ve done to date.
The Range Rumble is quite a gravel odyssey, but in a feat of route-planning genius, the most technical riding comes in the first half while you’re still fresh, and the last 20km or so is downhill — you can get pretty close to breaking the sound barrier down Mt Lindesay Road.
Expect to get your feet wet through the creek crossings, start doing those hill repeats and come prepared with the widest tyres your bike can handle — you won’t regret it.
For a slightly shorter option, the Wellington Rocks course follows the same route out of town as the Range Rumble but cuts out the outer portion of the loop through Boonoo Boonoo National Park.
This gives you a good bit of the Range Rumble experience, with all the techy goodness and scenery, but shaves off the most gruelling climbing around the outer reaches of the course. It also means that if you sign up for the Range Rumble but decide you need to pull the ripcord, there is a bailout at about 35km in.
At 38km long, the Saddlers MTB Club has flagged the Basket Swamp Bash as an adaptive-friendly option. While someone riding a Bowhead or similar a-MTB would likely make it through most of the terrain on the longer courses, a few of the creek crossings may not be passable on an adaptive bike.
The Basket Swamp Bash is roughly half gravel and half paved, and you’ll encounter one unavoidable creek crossing. It has a solid concrete base with about 30cm of water, so embrace the adventure and hit it at speed for a nice cool down.
Starting at Lindrook Road, about 20km from the showground, the Basket Swamp Bash takes on a breathtaking loop of the national park before running back towards town. Plus, you’ll get the same rip-roaring descent home, down Mt Lindesay Road.
After the event, the Saddlers MTB Club will run a shuttle back to the start so folks can pick up their cars if need be. However, space will be limited, and Reid recommends getting a ride out there if you can.
Last but certainly not least is the Currys Gap Family Ride. Taking place on Sunday morning, this 11km tour heads out from the showground and loops through the Currys Gap State Conservation Area.
The ride kicks off with a rolling start behind a lead vehicle to Currys Gap, which is also home to some of the new mountain bike trails. However, Reid says this loop will stick to the smooth gravel fire road.
With an approachable circuit, it’s a great opportunity to get your family involved in the weekend’s festivities. At the last Gravel ‘n Granite we saw a few kiddos loaded up on Kids Ride Shotgun seats, a heap of families, and plenty of folks new to the sport and wanting to see what this whole gravel thing is about.
Tenterfield is a leafy, wonderful little town in the Granite Belt, and by March the autumn colours should be starting to pop.
By the time that Gravel ‘n Granite rolls around, Reid tells us that the first 30km of the Angry Bull Trails will be open, so bring your mountain bike and stay for a few days to check out the singletrack.
Tenterfield has quite a few hotels, cottages, homestays, and Airbnbs, but we highly recommend camping at the showground.
That puts you within metres of the start/finish line, and before and after the race there was a strong community vibe with everyone hanging out and making friends.
The showground is within walking distance of town, and Reid says that heaps of the pubs will have live music on across the weekend.
If you would like to camp, you can book a site through the Saddlers MTB Club website when you enter.
On Friday (March 5) the night before the event, the Saddlers MTB Club is throwing a street party with live music, buskers, food trucks, and more.
After the event, there is heaps to explore in the national parks and state conservation areas surrounding Tenterfield and plenty to do in town too.
